transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-26
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Martinez (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Mariner Head of Platform), Sara Kim (Mariner CTO), Diego Ruiz (Mariner Cloud Architect)

Summary:
Quick intro between Redwood partnerships and Mariner Compute. High-level partner fit discussion (channel, joint go-to-market), technical alignment (bare metal GPU offerings, NVLink, multi-tenant vs dedicated racks), and initial ask: run a benchmarking pilot for Redwood Dedicated integration with Mariner's GPU fleet.

Topics:
- Partner program basics and commercial models
- Technical integration points: networking, VPC peering, KMS, audit logs
- Benchmarking: quantization, batching, throughput/latency targets
- Next steps and owners

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. I'm Alex from Redwood, AE on partnerships. With me is Priya, our solutions engineer.
[00:08] Priya: Hi all, hi. I'll mostly talk tech and benchmarks if we need to later.
[00:12] Liam: Thanks Alex, thanks Priya. I'm Liam, head of platform at Mariner. Sara and Diego are here from our side. We're excited to learn more.
[00:20] Sara: Hi. We're doing a push to partner with vendors who can help our customers run LLM workloads on-prem and hybrid.
[00:27] Diego: Hi all, small intro — I'm Diego, cloud architect. We run a mix of A100 and newer H100-class nodes, some RDMA NVLink clusters, also a managed Kubernetes layer.
[00:36] Alex: Great, that lines up. Quick Redwood overview: we provide hosted API, dedicated reserved pools for enterprise, and private deployments. On the partner side we do channel & integration partnerships where infra partners can host Redwood Dedicated or integrate via private control plane.
[00:52] Liam: And for commercial — how does Redwood typically handle revenue? Is it referral, rev share, or reseller?
[00:57] Alex: We do a few models; for infra partners it's often margin + referral, sometimes reseller where the partner invoices the customer and Redwood takes a platform fee. We'll send our partner one-pager after.
[01:08] Sara: Cool. From a product fit standpoint, our customers want low-latency inference with predictable unit economics. They ask for per-token cost guarantees for batch workloads — is that a Redwood thing?
[01:18] Priya: Yes — we optimize via batching, prefix KV caching, and quantization profiles. We also have tooling (Optimize) that suggests batching and quantization per workload. For Dedicated we can provision reserved pools which gives you predictable throughput.
[01:30] Diego: When you say KV caching, do you mean like a prefix cache persisted across requests? How does that play with multi-tenant?
[01:36] Priya: Right, prefix or KV cache. There are some trade-offs — with multi-tenant you need isolation so we typically do per-tenant cache shards or dedicate cache nodes. On Prem we can work with you to map cache pools to physical racks.
[01:50] Liam: On the networking side, what are the options? VPC peering, private link, or do you require something else?
[01:55] Alex: For private deployments we support VPC peering and private endpoints; on-prem we can run a customer-managed control plane with secure tunnels. We integrate with KMS/HSM for key management.
[02:06] Sara: SOC2 and audit logs — our customers want to see those. Do you provide SOC2 artifacts and retain audit logs?
[02:12] Alex: Yes we have SOC2, ISO in our enterprise pack; we can provide security pack and network diagrams. We'll exchange those docs after.
[02:20] Diego: One technical thing — our infra uses Slurm for job scheduling on bare metal for some clusters. Do you have experience integrating with cluster schedulers?
[02:28] Priya: We've integrated with Slurm and also Kubernetes via device plugins. For Slurm we typically build a scheduling adapter that handles capacity signaling and GPU allocation. It can be a bit bespoke but we've done it for other partners.
[02:40] Liam: Latency SLAs — what numbers are realistic for, say, a 2k token turn on A100?
[02:46] Priya: Depends on model family and quantization. For a 7B-ish open model quantized to 4-bit we could target single-digit 100s ms for short contexts, but for 2k tokens end-to-end latency will be higher. Our dashboards break down token latency and you can set routing policies for low-latency tiers.
[03:03] Sara: On model variants — do you handle fallbacks automatically? For example if capacity is constrained on Mariner infra, can requests spill to Redwood hosted or other pools?
[03:11] Alex: Yes, smart routing supports policy-based failover — you can route by latency, cost, region, and fallback to compatible model variants or hosted fallback.
[03:22] Diego: For security, can we keep customer data on-prem always? We need to keep KV and audit trails inside the customer's network for certain regulated customers.
[03:31] Priya: Absolutely — private deployment lets you manage the control plane and keep logs and data in your VPC or on-prem. We can also encrypt with your KMS.
[03:39] Liam: For benchmarking, what's the typical rubric? We want throughput and cost per token, but also memory/PCIe utilization.
[03:46] Priya: We'll propose a benchmark suite: latency p50/p95/p99, throughput (tokens/sec) for steady state and burst, GPU utilization, PCIe and NVLink usage, and cold start behaviors. We'll include quantized and FP16 runs.
[03:59] Alex: And we'll also want a simple integration test — sample inference endpoints, a small dataset for quality checks, and a spreadsheet to capture results. We'll share a benchmark rubric and sample scripts.
[04:10] Sara: One quick commercial Q — are you open to joint marketing for the pilot? Co-branded case studies?
[04:14] Alex: Yes, if the pilot goes well we typically do a joint case study and partner listing.
[04:18] Diego: Any gotchas on the infra side? We worry about model compilation time for new model variants.
[04:24] Priya: Compilation can take time; we cache compiled kernels and reuse. For new model families we usually do a one-time compile step and we can do cross-checks in an isolated env. We'll also test quantized variants to reduce runtime.
[04:36] Liam: Sounds good. How long does it take to stand up a Dedicated pool on partner infra?
[04:40] Alex: From order to first traffic typically 4-6 weeks, depends on network setup and security reviews. For pilots we can sometimes shortcut with smaller test pools in 1-2 weeks.
[04:50] Diego: Diego: (mumbled) question about billing metering — do you surface token-level metering if we resell?
[04:56] Alex: Yes, our billing APIs provide token-level usage and cost attribution per tenant. You can integrate that into your billing stack.
[05:04] Sara: Great. Any competitors you see in this space that we should be aware of?
[05:08] Alex: There are infra providers and some vendors like Lambda Labs and Paperspace who do similar infra, plus cloud providers. But Redwood's differentiator is the unified runtime and routing + cost controls.
[05:20] Liam: Ok next steps — sounds like exchanging docs and scheduling a technical deep dive.
[05:24] Alex: Agreed. Priya, can you lead the tech deep dive?
[05:28] Priya: Yep, I'll propose slots next week.
[05:30] Sara: We'll pull infra inventory and a couple sample customer use-cases to share.
[05:33] Alex: Perfect. We'll follow up with the partner one-pager, security pack, and a benchmark rubric.
[05:39] Diego: Quick clarifying note — when you say dedicated pools, are they hard-partitioned nodes or soft-shared with isolation?
[05:45] Priya: They can be hard-partitioned for strict isolation; or soft-shared with per-tenant scheduler and QoS guarantees. It's configurable.
[05:55] Liam: Any requests from your side for us to prepare before the deep dive?
[05:58] Alex: The infra inventory (node types, interconnect, scheduler), network topology, and a point of contact for security.
[06:05] Sara: We'll get that together. Thanks everyone.
[06:08] Alex: Thanks — we'll send notes and next steps.

Notes on transcript quality: automated transcription had a few mis-hears ("KV cash" for KV cache, "Slurm" sometimes to "slorm") and occasional speaker label confusion.
